The plan is written and committed as `docs/hosted-machine-plan.md` (commit `1ccc21b`), with a link from `standalone-product.md`. Nothing has been built and no AWS resources exist.

1. **Substrate:** EC2 t4g.xlarge (arm64, 4 vCPU, 16 GiB) in us-east-1, at $118.76/month, or $91.39 with a 1-year Savings Plan. Lightsail can't use an instance IAM role for Secrets Manager. Extending Forge would take an estimated 30–60 engineer-days.
2. **Fixes first:** Unfixed, three known defects cost more than the machine. Thread-list refetching would add $108–252/month in AWS egress, and backend CPU overhead $34–57/month. Memory also grows without bound.
3. **Connectivity:** Tailscale only, with no inbound ports, and the server stays bound to loopback. The phone pairs with the machine directly. The desktop uses an SSH tunnel and shows "Hosted · <name>", taken from what the server reports about itself.
4. **Browser:** one shared headless Chromium on the machine, driven through Playwright MCP. You log in or enter a 2FA code once through a DevTools screencast over SSH. On macOS, logins survived a browser restart, and screencast plus typed input worked.
5. **Linux readiness:** the server ran headless in an Ubuntu 24.04 arm64 container. The full test suite there was cut short, so the Linux test result comes from CI (x86_64, 1,561 tests passing on Oct 26).
6. **Not measured:** the local Docker probes filled this Mac's disk, so the full arm64 suite, Chromium on Linux, build CPU and provider login prompts were never run. Phase 1 measures them on the real machine. I've quit Docker, as it was before the session; the Mac has only about 6 GB free.
7. **Independent review:** a fresh Codex agent found 14 real issues, all now in the plan. The worst were agents reading the Tailscale key and SSH host keys through the instance role, and an agent rewriting Tailscale Serve to skip phone pairing.
8. **Estimate:** about 18–29 engineer-days across five phases, ending in a 10-step acceptance script.

I need your approval, plus answers to the 13 open questions at the end of the plan. The most important are how far to restrict your tailnet policy, whether to enable Antigravity, and whether agents may have sudo.

The I18 change now reduces what opening a conversation transfers, not just what it renders. It is delivered to the reviewer, release owner and parent, but the reviewer hasn't approved it yet, so I haven't sent the final campaign reply.

**What changed:** opening a conversation now asks for a "recent view": the latest 40 turns, with long tool outputs in finished turns cut to short previews. Your messages, the agent's replies, reasoning, plans and any running turn are never cut. "Show N earlier turns", a new "Show full output" button, search results and message links load the complete history. The saved history is never modified. A backend that doesn't know the request header just sends everything, as before.

**Why the previews matter:** across 549 real saved conversations, the size comes from tool output, not turn count. One was 22 MB in only 2 turns, so a 40-turn limit alone would have saved almost nothing.

**Measured on 4 real conversations, 7 opens each per view, same code:**

| Turns | Bytes (recent vs complete) | Median time to Send enabled |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 0.10 vs 0.84 MB | 189 vs 191 ms |
| 38 | 3.0 vs 4.6 MB | 268 vs 335 ms |
| 93 | 2.4 vs 8.2 MB | 411 vs 525 ms |
| 67 | 3.7 vs 11.9 MB | 652 vs 787 ms |

- **Timings are under load:** the live runtime and an unrelated `ramble_bench` job were running (load average about 13), so the timings are not clean absolute numbers. I reported the overlap to the parent while it happened.
- **Smaller gain than bytes:** time to Send improves less than bytes do, because the server still reads and copies the complete history on every open.
- **Opens and checks:** all 56 opens succeeded with no errors. In a real browser, earlier turns, full output and a search result in an early turn all work, and Send stays enabled.
- **Tests:** all 1,090 JS tests and the 266 focused Python tests pass with the change applied to the release owner's preserved source. Nine of the 10 new JS tests fail without the change, as they should.

**A bug I found in my earlier reviewed change:** opening a search result more than 40 turns back could wrongly say the message was "no longer available". This delta fixes it.

**Not fixed:**
- **First search after a backend start:** 0.8–1.1 s, over the 800 ms budget. About 300 ms of that is re-indexing conversations that changed since the last search; the rest is cold caches. Later searches take 68–137 ms. Fixing it means a background indexer that would need its own measurement, so I left it as the parent's decision.
- **Conversations with thousands of tool calls:** still 2–5 MB on open.

**Other things you should know:**
- **Orphaned harness backend:** a measurement backend from one of my earlier runs kept running in the background for about 4 minutes at roughly 15% CPU. I stopped it, told the release owner, and changed the harness so this can't recur.
- **The command you rejected:** it was a recursive delete of my own scratch folder, with the path computed from a file. I redid the work without deleting anything and will avoid that pattern.
- **Release owner's copy:** I gave them an exact, read-only copy of my reviewed files, with my changes separated from other teams' edits to the same files. They verified it.
- **Permission-mode team's patch:** at their request I applied their patch to the main working tree; the focused tests pass.

Everything is in `build/responsiveness/perf-campaign/i18-transfer/delivery-20261029T2045Z/` (start with `DELIVERY.txt`). No full test suite, build, install, plugin refresh or git change was made.

## Short answer

Your agents were told two opposite things about Git. About a dozen of them then edited one shared copy of the repo at the same time, and the build and install tools package whatever is in that copy. Once the copy stopped being trustworthy, the release work moved into private snapshots that were never merged back into main. Nothing was lost or deleted: `history_window.py` was never in the working tree in the first place.

## The chain of causes

**1. Every session is told not to use Git.** The beads startup hook (`bd prime` for Claude, `bd codex-hook SessionStart` for Codex) injects "Git authority: no git operations in this context" into every session. The beads block in CLAUDE.md agrees: by default, don't commit unless explicitly asked. Separately, `da76ba8` (Oct 15) added "Commit your changes once you are done." Neither instruction overrides the other, so agents split. The UI agents committed. The reliability orchestrator (`01a1888b`) followed the hook, and told you at 15:03 and 15:18: "Commit/push is also restricted by the current no-Git hook." It never asked you to settle the conflict. You didn't choose the no-Git rule: `no-git-ops` isn't set in `.beads/config.yaml`, so this is beads' default output.

**2. About 12 agents shared one working tree.** At 13:03 you asked that orchestrator to "launch yolo app agents to fix all of those issues. make sure we independently review and validate them." They all edited `/opt/projects/agent-coord` on main. `begin-work` scopes stop two agents editing the same file at once, but they don't keep each agent's changes separate.

**3. The tools treat the working tree as the release.** `build.py` copies `plugins/agent-coord/scripts/agent_coord/` from disk, and the plugin installer does the same. At 13:15 an install probe copied the in-progress tree, including unreviewed edits, into the live plugin cache that every running agent's hooks use. The recovery rule written afterwards was "No plugin add/refresh from moving working tree." From that point, the working tree couldn't be trusted as a source.

**4. Independent review needs a fixed version to review.** With no commits, the only way to say "this is the version I approved" was a copy plus a list of file hashes. That's where the `build/<task>/{base,work,candidate,patch,manifest.json}` folders came from: 19 GB in total, 4.4 GB for the release folder.

**5. The release was built from those copies, not from main.**
- **14:50:** the release owner's `capture_candidate.py` (its description: "Preserve source without git or changing the shared working tree") copied the working tree. It copied every file on disk, committed or not.
- **Picked up:** `conversation_residency.py` and `inventory_projection.py` were created at 13:25, before the copy. That's why they're installed but still untracked.
- **Missed:** `permission_modes.py` (15:19) and `execution_state.py` (15:51) were created after the copy, so they're in neither the build nor main.
- **Built only from the copy:** the recent-history work (`history_window.py`) was written in `i18-transfer/work` on top of the 14:50 copy. It was handed over as a patch against that copy and never touched the shared tree. Its delivery notes say "Full suite not run (not authorized)."
- **Build lineage:** build 19 came from that copy after six rounds of added patches. Build 20 is build 19's source plus the deferred-message change.

**6. Commits were assembled outside the working tree.** The deferred-message agent committed `ff6322d`, `d0aa572` and `07c3dbd` through a separate Git index (a private staging file), using its own copies of the files. So five of the files in `07c3dbd` still show as modified on disk, because the shared copies also hold other agents' changes. For example, `store.py` differs by +104/−27 lines and `browser_wake.py` by +219/−29.

**7. Nobody was assigned to merge it back.** The release status file lists its pending items, and none of them is "land this in main." The release agent was retired at 16:44. Separately, `8b5e5d4` has been sitting on its own branch since Oct 28.

## On the second analysis you pasted

Most of it is right: 79 changed files mixing finished, half-done and cancelled work; building from them would ship everything; agents reassembling clean versions by hand; 48 folders taking 19 GB.

One claim is wrong. "No instructions tell them to do this" is true only of the folder layout. An instruction not to use Git is injected into every session, and the orchestrator cited it by name. The 13:15 incident added a second rule against building from the working tree. With "don't commit", "don't trust the shared tree" and "review independently" all in force, snapshot folders were the only option left. Also, it says there are no other branches or worktrees, but there is exactly one: `fix/scope-overlap-interrupted-recovery`.

## What would stop it recurring

1. **Pick one Git rule.** I'd keep "commit when done" and stop beads from saying otherwise. Overriding beads' startup text with a `.beads/PRIME.md` file is its documented mechanism.
2. **Give each concurrent agent its own worktree and branch.** Agent Coord already treats linked worktrees as part of the same repository.
3. **Build and install from a named commit, not from disk,** and record that commit inside the app.
4. **Reconcile once, with a single owner.** Land as commits:
   - the recent-history patch;
   - the residency and projection modules;
   - the permission and approval modules;
   - `8b5e5d4`.

   Drop the cancelled window-restoration edits, then rebuild from that commit.

I haven't changed anything. Do you want me to start the reconciliation, or fix the Git rule first?

**What went into main:** everything that existed only in the working tree or only in the build 22 source, merged with main's own commits:

**How I checked nothing was lost:**
- Every line added by main, the working tree, and builds 19, 20 and 22 is present in the result. The one exception is the earlier 40-turn timeline windowing, which build 22's reviewed recent-history work replaced.

- Python: 1967 tests pass. The first run had 27 failures, all caused by my session's identity variables leaking into the tests; a clean environment fixes them, the same way the other agents validated. I saved that as a beads memory.
- JavaScript: 1120 of 1120 tests pass, and all the plugin and skill validators pass.

**Kept out of main, but saved on branches:**
- **`archive/window-restoration`:** the cancelled work, complete and on top of the new main. Its final native rerun and full suite were never done.
- **`integration/capacity-retry`:** capacity retry merged onto the new main. It passes 1999 Python and 1121 JavaScript tests. I didn't merge it because its handoff requires an independent review after rebasing, since it adds automatic turn retries. Two conflicts needed judgment: it now uses the newer exact-turn Stop check to decide whether a stop was deliberate, and the hook delivers both deferred messages and retry context. Those two are what the reviewer should look at.
- **`fix/scope-overlap-interrupted-recovery`:** left as is. Its scope fix is already in main, and the older recovery half was deliberately not imported because the newer Stop safeguards replace it.

Every original input (working tree, captures, builds 19/20/22) is also saved under `refs/preserve/reconcile-20261029/*`, plus a tarball at `/tmp/rf_reconcile/worktree-changes-20261029.tgz`.

**Not done, and each needs your go-ahead:**
- Pushing: main is 37 commits ahead of GitHub.
- Refreshing the installed plugin caches from main: this changes every running agent's hooks.
- Building and installing an app from `3368b3b`.

evidence.text:
Yes. **The earlier fixes addressed real problems, but never established one bounded database writer.** I checked the commits, compared the relevant installed code with the repository, and reproduced two remaining defects.

**What causes it**

1. **One runtime process still contains competing writers.** Commit `c1255ef`, “Serialize runtime mutations,” routes operations into the runtime. But its [ownership check](/opt/projects/agent-coord/plugins/agent-coord/scripts/agent_coord/runtime_requests.py:65) bypasses the mutex once that process owns the database. HTTP handlers, provider persistence and background workers then use separate writable connections concurrently.

2. **Some transactions hold the writer lock through substantial computation.** [Search indexing](/opt/projects/agent-coord/plugins/agent-coord/scripts/agent_coord/conversation_search.py:106) acquires the lock, fetches every dirty conversation, parses its JSON, extracts messages and rebuilds the index before committing. There is no byte or time limit. Search and dispatcher requests both invoke this synchronously.

3. **Saving history amplifies the work.** Persistence replaces the complete conversation and invalidates its search projection. Your database contains about **2.28 GB of saved histories**, with individual histories reaching **37 MB**. One observed indexing backlog contained roughly **87 MB** of history.

I reproduced both competing runtime writers and search parsing blocking an unrelated write in an isolated database. The relevant fixes **are installed**; this recurrence is not explained by an old backend.

**Why the previous fixes didn’t solve it**

| Commits | What they improved | What remained |
|---|---|---|
| `7622cff` | Removed unnecessary writes; returned useful busy errors | Competing writers still existed |
| `ddf9968`, `31fda65` | Kept jobs and Claude alive during contention | Recovery rather than prevention |
| `1f949aa`, `097634c` | Reduced polling, connection overhead and interface latency | Long write transactions remained |
| `c1255ef`, `6201a6b` | Centralized process ownership and fixed startup races | No serialization among the owner’s threads |

**The tests missed the distinction.** They tested serialization in the *standalone* path, where the mutex works. They also tested reads surviving held writers and eventual recovery. They did not prove that concurrent runtime-owned writes remain bounded. The earlier load test’s six synthetic agents and short run demonstrated improvement under that workload.

**How we actually solve it**

1. **Give the runtime one explicit writer executor.** Every mutation passes through it. Queue finite database transactions; keep provider calls, network waits and expensive preparation outside it. A mutex around whole requests would introduce another blocking problem.

2. **Prepare search updates outside write transactions.** Read a history revision, calculate its projection, then publish a bounded batch. Clear its dirty marker only if that revision still matches, preserving updates that arrive during indexing.

3. **Persist changed items or turns incrementally.** Avoid rewriting and reindexing an entire growing conversation after small changes. Coalesce replaceable snapshots and heartbeats; give submission receipts and lifecycle changes bounded service.

4. **Make this a release gate.** Exercise the actual runtime-owner path with large histories, concurrent submissions, indexing and background writes. Verify submission latency, durable outcomes, restart recovery and absence of writer starvation.

5. **Record transaction identity and duration.** Measure queue delay, lock duration and backlog so the next incident identifies its blocker directly.

The existing logs cannot identify the **exact transaction behind your screenshot**. The structural defects above are reproduced, however, and explain why repeated contention remains possible.

[Reproduction script](/Users/walle/.local/state/agent-coord/diagnostics/database_contention_20261102/reproduce_database_contention.py). The proposed redesign has not yet been implemented.

Independent initial assessment, read-only. Worktree /tmp/agent-coord-uninterrupted is clean at eca4133 (no implementer commits yet); harness and fixture are byte-identical to main; installed runtime (pid 49958, payload a945946f) runs a desktop_runtime.py identical to the worktree copy. Nothing in the live runtime was touched. Line numbers below are worktree files under plugins/agent-coord/scripts/agent_coord unless noted.

1. Refuting a PID-preserving facade. The gate cannot currently tell a facade from a real successor: runtime_live_acceptance.py:178/186 assert only Path(status["payload"]).name == digest; the ACCEPTANCE_PAYLOAD_GENERATION marker written at :103 is never read back; before/after status (including pid) is recorded at :184 but never compared. A new payload that attaches, rewrites selected.json/discovery payload and proxies HTTP to the old process passes every check. Why a facade cannot meet the user bar: all live-turn state is process-local to the old coordinator: CodexRPC.pending and the blocking line reader (codex_app_server.py:155-186), BrowserSessions.requests/active/histories/events/sequence (:176-213), ClaudeRPC.turns/requests/connections and ClaudeConnection.pending (claude_code.py:119-150, 476, 684). Approval replies are written with the provider-native request id via self._rpc(thread_id) (codex_app_server.py:2571-2618), so whoever holds the pipe must also hold the request table. Provider close() terminates processes (codex_app_server.py:187-197; claude_code.py:151-158). Required gate strengthening (does not weaken anything): assert status pid changes per swap and that an in-process identity value (e.g. the generation marker echoed by identity/status) matches the expected payload, and assert the observer's post-activation HTTP responses come from the new pid.

2. Strongest feasible mechanism. Same-host descriptor transfer of each provider's stdin/stdout/stderr pipe ends over a Unix socket (socket.send_fds; installed interpreter is 3.12.7 per backend.json, so available) plus a JSON session snapshot taken with the reader thread parked at a frame boundary: per transport {pending request ids with thread/turn, unparsed partial-line buffer, outstanding approval requests keyed by provider request id to UI key, active turn ids, decoder state}, plus the event sequence counter and deque tail, queue owner id, and admission state. The predecessor must exit via os._exit without running _close_components (codex_app_server.py:2620+) or the reader finally block (:177-186), which would mark turns failed and pause queues (:832-850) unless runtime_handover is set. Evidence this is feasible: build/live-runtime-fd-spike/results/summary.json clean scenario 20/20 conserved, same_pid 20/20, duplicate frames 0, handover stall p95 0.9 ms, activation p95 52 ms; partial_frame_runs 14/20 shows the partial-line buffer must travel. This is strictly more than Envoy hot restart (which does not transfer established connections); systemd fd-store and Erlang release handling are the closer precedents.

3. Essential invariants.
 a. Command receipt: a command is accepted only when the frame is written to the provider pipe and its request id is in the transferred pending table, or its response has been applied. browser_queue._dispatch claims queued->sending (browser_queue.py:188) before sessions.send(start_only=True) (:195) and deletes after; a crash between claim and provider write strands the row under the dead owner uuid (:19, :52-53). Exactly-once then degrades to zero-times; the gate should fail that correctly. Persist the provider request id with the row before writing the frame (write-ahead receipt) so the successor can distinguish sent from unsent.
 b. Projection/cursor atomicity: delta application item[field] += delta (codex_app_server.py ~985) is not idempotent, so a replayed frame duplicates text and a dropped frame leaves a gap. The frame cursor (last consumed provider line per transport) and the projection (histories/items, active turn) must be committed in one snapshot with no reader progress in between. events_after (:1115-1120) returns reset whenever the successor starts with sequence 0 or an empty deque; the successor must inherit sequence and the deque tail, or the SSE client must tolerate reset without re-rendering.
 c. Original approval: request table transfers with provider-native ids; otherwise answer raises "no longer pending" and the fixture waits forever (fixture :88), which is the right failure.
 d. No disconnect emission for transferred transports in either process; no terminate on transferred children. coordinate_update may killpg(source_pid) after 30 s (desktop_runtime.py:961); Codex children use start_new_session=True (codex_app_server.py:101) but any provider still in the source process group would die. Assert provider pgid != source pgid.

4. Failure-injection cases missing from scripts/runtime_live_acceptance.py.
 - Tool-child SIGKILL is invisible. Executable counterexample: python3 build/live-runtime-gate-review/probe_tool_child_sigkill_undetected.py drives the fixture alone, kills the tool child; checks at :193, :195, :210 all pass while tool_complete.returncode is -9 and no tool_exit record exists. Add: tool_complete.returncode == 0, one tool_exit per tool_start, item/completed exitCode 0.
 - Provider killed and not respawned leaves no record (fixture handles only TERM/INT/HUP, :45). Add end-of-run liveness assertion for each original provider pid (isolated pids only).
 - observer_errors (:143-144) are reported (:247) but never asserted; HTTP outages shorter than the 5 s stall window pass. Assert zero.
 - SSE continuity unmeasured: observer polls REST (:140). Add an /api/browser/events consumer with Last-Event-ID asserting no reset and contiguous seq across all swaps.
 - No command arriving mid-swap: steer, approval reply, queue dispatch, scheduled wake, inbox wake during the handover window; exactly-once is measured only for queued-after-stream.
 - No handover crash injection: kill candidate before commit, kill predecessor after descriptor transfer but before exit, kill during snapshot, kill both; the fd-spike scenarios kill_old_sent/kill_candidate_* are a model.
 - Approval request presence/key not re-verified per swap (only activeTurn at :190); the original key must remain answerable after every swap.
 - Pid capture race: provider_ids is taken at :164 after tool_pid (fixture :97) but the child writes its own start record later (fixture :180); wait for it or the pid-set check fails spuriously.
 - Report keeps no provider.jsonl or runtime log copy; swap activation measures status polling only, not provide

Executable counterexample: python3 build/live-runtime-gate-review/probe_tool_child_sigkill_undetected.py drives the fixture alone, kills the tool child; checks at :193, :195, :210 all pass while tool_complete.returncode is -9 and no tool_exit record exists.  - Provider killed and not respawned leaves no record (fixture handles only TERM/INT/HUP, :45). Add end-of-run liveness assertion for each original provider pid (isolated pids only).
 - observer_errors (:143-144) are reported (:247) but never asserted; HTTP outages shorter than the 5 s stall window pass. Assert zero.

Its control surface (identity, client-request, activate-update, attach, decision, pause, resume, stop; desktop_runtime.py:592-661) exposes no descriptor export or state snapshot, hands over only when readiness() is empty (:786) or when update_requested with no inflight admissions (:791/:828), and its shutdown terminates providers. evidence.text:
Your screenshot was the key clue. The Mac is out of memory, and Ribbon Field (RF) is the main reason. A wasteful backend makes it worse. I haven't changed any code yet.

## Why it's slow

**1. Memory is exhausted, and RF uses most of it.** The machine has 16 GB of RAM and **27.9 of 28.7 GB of swap in use**, so everything is paging. RF's own processes add up to about 16.6 GB:

| Process | Memory |
|---|---|
| Ribbon Field Networking (WebKit) | **8.7 GB**, all of it WebKit's own allocations |
| `codex app-server` (started by RF, up 47 h) | 4.9 GB |
| WebKit page content process | 1.5 GB |
| Python backend | 1.4 GB |

The 8.7 GB looks like WebKit holding on to RF's three live event streams, one per open window. Those connections have been open for about 47 hours and have delivered about 7.8 GB, which nearly matches the memory size. Over 90 seconds the memory grew 6 MB while the streams sent 3.4 MB, and about 67 MB of ordinary responses in the same window were not kept. That is a strong correlation but not proof yet. `python3.12` (PID 66830) in your screenshot is your Ramble benchmark job, not RF, but it adds to the pressure.

**2. The backend has been at 220–300% CPU for two days, mostly re-reading the database.** About 74% of its on-CPU samples are disk page reads and 13% are writes. The causes:
- **A fresh SQLite connection for every operation** (`store.py:246`). Each one re-parses the 170-object schema and starts with an empty cache. Around 15 background loops run every 0.25–2 s; one of them (`inbox_wake`) runs 379 statements, taking up to 572 ms, every 0.5 s.
- **Whole conversation histories rewritten on every tool call.** `browser_history` is 1.42 GB of the 1.6 GB database, with single conversations up to 35 MB. The full blob is rewritten each time an item completes. Other writers then wait up to about 0.9 s for the database lock (p99).
- **Full scans of `app_control_requests`** (27 MB, no indexes at all), repeated per thread.

**3. The UI keeps re-fetching the whole thread list.** Almost every streamed event, including each tool start and finish (`app.js:1988`), re-fetches the full list. That request takes **0.7–1.6 s and returns 4.5 MB**. Most of the size is each card's full original prompt (37%), links (26%) and checkpoint (20%). Opening your largest conversation takes **18.8 s and transfers 36.9 MB**.

## Best way to address it

1. **Now, no code needed:** reload each RF window with Cmd-R. This only reloads the page; the backend and your agents keep running. If Ribbon Field Networking drops from 8.7 GB, that confirms the stream cause and frees roughly 8 GB of swap. A full app restart would also free the Codex server's 4.9 GB, but it interrupts running agents.
2. **First fix (small, highest leverage):** have the server close each event stream after a few minutes. The browser reconnects within about 1.5 s and resumes where it left off, which the server already supports. This caps WebKit's memory whatever the underlying WebKit cause.
3. **Second fix (small):** refresh the thread list only for events that change it, not tool and hook events (about 75% of the stream). Also send a short preview instead of the full prompt, links and checkpoint in list cards.
4. **Then the backend:**
   - Reuse SQLite connections instead of opening one per operation.
   - Add an index on `app_control_requests(thread_id, operation)`.
   - Save each history at most every few seconds and at turn end, instead of on every item.
5. **Later:** load long conversations a page at a time instead of all 37 MB, and look at why the Codex server reaches 4.9 GB.

Your screenshot was the key clue. The Mac is out of memory, and Ribbon Field (RF) is the main reason. A wasteful backend makes it worse. I haven't changed any code yet.

## Why it's slow

**1. Memory is exhausted, and RF uses most of it.** The machine has 16 GB of RAM and **27.9 of 28.7 GB of swap in use**, so everything is paging. RF's own processes add up to about 16.6 GB:

| Process | Memory |
|---|---|
| Ribbon Field Networking (WebKit) | **8.7 GB**, all of it WebKit's own allocations |
| `codex app-server` (started by RF, up 47 h) | 4.9 GB |
| WebKit page content process | 1.5 GB |
| Python backend | 1.4 GB |

The 8.7 GB looks like WebKit holding on to RF's three live event streams, one per open window. Those connections have been open for about 47 hours and have delivered about 7.8 GB, which nearly matches the memory size. Over 90 seconds the memory grew 6 MB while the streams sent 3.4 MB, and about 67 MB of ordinary responses in the same window were not kept. That is a strong correlation but not proof yet. `python3.12` (PID 66830) in your screenshot is your Ramble benchmark job, not RF, but it adds to the pressure.

**2. The backend has been at 220–300% CPU for two days, mostly re-reading the database.** About 74% of its on-CPU samples are disk page reads and 13% are writes. The causes:
- **A fresh SQLite connection for every operation** (`store.py:246`). Each one re-parses the 170-object schema and starts with an empty cache. Around 15 background loops run every 0.25–2 s; one of them (`inbox_wake`) runs 379 statements, taking up to 572 ms, every 0.5 s.
- **Whole conversation histories rewritten on every tool call.** `browser_history` is 1.42 GB of the 1.6 GB database, with single conversations up to 35 MB. The full blob is rewritten each time an item completes. Other writers then wait up to about 0.9 s for the database lock (p99).
- **Full scans of `app_control_requests`** (27 MB, no indexes at all), repeated per thread.

**3. The UI keeps re-fetching the whole thread list.** Almost every streamed event, including each tool start and finish (`app.js:1988`), re-fetches the full list. That request takes **0.7–1.6 s and returns 4.5 MB**. Most of the size is each card's full original prompt (37%), links (26%) and checkpoint (20%). Opening your largest conversation takes **18.8 s and transfers 36.9 MB**.

## Best way to address it

1. **Now, no code needed:** reload each RF window with Cmd-R. This only reloads the page; the backend and your agents keep running. If Ribbon Field Networking drops from 8.7 GB, that confirms the stream cause and frees roughly 8 GB of swap. A full app restart would also free the Codex server's 4.9 GB, but it interrupts running agents.
2. **First fix (small, highest leverage):** have the server close each event stream after a few minutes. The browser reconnects within about 1.5 s and resumes where it left off, which the server already supports. This caps WebKit's memory whatever the underlying WebKit cause.
3. **Second fix (small):** refresh the thread list only for events that change it, not tool and hook events (about 75% of the stream). Also send a short preview instead of the full prompt, links and checkpoint in list cards.
4. **Then the backend:**
   - Reuse SQLite connections instead of opening one per operation.
   - Add an index on `app_control_requests(thread_id, operation)`.
   - Save each history at most every few seconds and at turn end, instead of on every item.
5. **Later:** load long conversations a page at a time instead of all 37 MB, and look at why the Codex server reaches 4.9 GB.

2. **Distinguish internal callback errors from an actual disconnect**, and log the exception with session and turn IDs.
3. **Add a Claude regression test** that locks SQLite during initialization, then verifies the final response survives, completion is recorded once, and the next queued message is delivered. Also verify genuine failures and deliberate stops retain their behavior.

The runtime owner problem is still happening on the live build 17 backend and is the only urgent defect; one claim (`shared-gil`) is weakened because one of its two citations doesn't back it. The full report is at `/private/tmp/rf-audit-review-20261029/report.md`, and the checkpoint is saved.

| runtime-identity | Holds; still happening on build 17 | **Urgent defect** |

| inventory-size | Holds; measured 5.87 MB live | Residual |
| cold-open | Holds | Residual |
| shared-gil | Weakened: one of its two citations doesn't support it | Residual |
| live-upgrades | Holds | Paused by the user, not a repair target |
| public-release | Holds; checked again at 16:57Z | Not published yet (user's decision) |
| test-feedback | Holds | Unfinished test-speed investigation |

**The three you asked about:**
- **Runtime owner problem:** It is still in the active code. The build 17 backend's owner-check files are identical to the repo. Checking the owner runs a full busy scan that waits on locks and the database, with a 2-second timeout. Any failure is then reported as "Refusing a second owner". It blocked real commands after build 17 went live:
  - an `agent-coord inbox` command at 16:36:49Z;
  - a Claude tool call at 16:51:04Z, blocked by the agent-coord hook.

  The backend log also shows two broken connections on the control server, which fits clients giving up after 2 seconds. One open question: the 16:36Z failure took only 6 ms, too fast for a timeout, so there may be a second failure path.
- **Idle-provider memory is not bounded.** There is no unload, eviction or cap code. The 24.3 GB figure came from an app version about two days older than this window, so it isn't a build 17 number. The live backend now has 136 processes and 1.86 GB after 9.5 hours. That is about 14 new processes an hour, the same rate as before, so the growth continues.
- **The WebKit change is mitigation only.** Commit `4b43720` cuts how often the UI makes requests, and its own message says WebKit keeps about 5.5 KB per request and never releases it. That slows growth but doesn't stop it. Live it is 148–157 MB after 10 hours (previously 8.7 GB at 47 hours). It sometimes drops, so it may oscillate rather than climb steadily.

**Dependencies between the proposed groups:**
1. The uncommitted startup-lock fix (`store.py`, `tests/test_store.py`) sits in the same working tree as the paused live-upgrade files. Whoever commits the fix must commit only those files.
2. A fix to the owner check on the client side takes effect with a plugin refresh. Server-side changes, including the `store.py` retry, only go live when the backend is idle, which ties the persistence fixes to the live-upgrades limitation.
3. Capping idle conversations would remove the fast path for sending to a loaded conversation, so first-open latency (up to 1.23 s live) comes back. The cap and latest-turn loading need to be designed together.
4. The 5.87 MB list is also built on the shared backend each time it isn't cached, so `inventory-size` affects `shared-gil` too, not just the web view.
5. Publishing 0.1.3 build 17 as it is would ship the owner defect to customers.
6. Missing from the inventory: branch `fix/scope-overlap-interrupted-recovery` (commit `8b5e5d4`) is unmerged, and a reproduction file from the wide audit (`scope-reproduction.json`) shows the active backend still has that scope-overlap bug. That team may already own it.

**Measurements still needed:**
- **Owner check:** hook latency versus busy-scan time, plus the exception type behind a failed owner check, to explain the 6 ms case.
- **Idle memory:** hourly memory and process counts against the number of loaded conversations.
- **WebKit:** a footprint sample every 5 minutes for at least 2 hours with windows open.
- **Public 0.1.2:** whether it points at the update feeds that now return 404. If so, current public users can't get updates.

| Group | Outstanding issues to keep together | Ownership recommendation |
|---|---|---|
| **A. Runtime, storage, scopes and hooks** | Healthy runtime rejected as unavailable when its ownership check blocks; SQLite startup retry/migration fix still unintegrated; false glob scope conflicts; nested-repository registration changes the base of an existing scope; actionable messages buried beyond the hook preview; blockers displayed as “New session.” | **One agent.** Reuse the [runtime investigator](agentcoord://thread/01a185f4-19a5-7e83-945f-f38f37a528c4), incorporating the existing storage and scope patches. These share `store.py`, hooks and write-policy behavior. |
| **B. Wake, recovery and thread lifecycle** | Old failure pauses survive deployment of the underlying fix; human-created leads lack creator-directed escalation; a database error during wake can leave an indefinite uncertain pause; unloaded retired workers never complete their close requests; automatic wake prompts are mistaken for human messages. | **One lifecycle agent.** Recovery, closure and escalation must agree about running, stopped, failed and uncertain work. Preserve deliberate Stops and avoid retrying work that may already have executed. |
| **C. Conversation UI** | Displayed default model rejected on first send; accepted messages obscured during compaction with misleading stopped status; HTML artifact links fail on phones. | **One UI integration owner, with sequential handoffs between existing specialists.** The [HTML-preview agent](agentcoord://thread/01a183db-d7e2-7dc0-a752-7c41934b97eb) started implementation during this audit and owns shared UI files. The [model-selection issue](agentcoord://thread/01a18885-47bb-7b50-ac7b-9cec989ed4b8) is already assigned. Compaction needs verification against the local-echo fix already shipped. |
| **D. Plugin and MCP tooling** | Plugin refresh temporarily removes hook paths used by existing sessions; checkpoint calls lack automatic caller identity; minor CLI diagnostics and response-contract friction, including misleading missing-job errors. | **A separate tooling agent.** Plugin installation and MCP work can proceed independently. Explicit `session_id` already works around the identity problem. Keep hook-message formatting with Group A. |
| **E. Memory and remaining performance work** | Idle conversations retain provider/MCP processes without a cap; WebKit request retention is mitigated but not bounded; inventory responses remain about **5.9 MB**; large first opens load full history; the shared backend saturates under increased load. | Reuse the [responsiveness owner](agentcoord://thread/ed695f49-366e-4612-8a51-81bebbf7e2ce) for this whole group. Eviction affects reopen latency; inventory traffic affects backend load and WebKit memory. These should be designed together. |
| **F. Public release** | The public manifest still lists **0.1.2/build 3**; alpha update feeds return 404. Local **0.1.3/build 17** and successful CI have not established a published customer update. | Keep the existing [release owner](agentcoord://thread/01a183b1-530e-7003-92fc-e221b6f8818f). Artifact preparation can run independently; final integration, installation and publication need one owner. |
| **G. Test turnaround** | The parallel-suite investigation remains unfinished: the faster run skipped additional crypto tests, so equivalent coverage has not been demonstrated. | Reuse the [test investigation](agentcoord://thread/01a185bd-3ace-7e70-b17a-6cdb48b582dc), independently of product repairs. Avoid running timing comparisons alongside heavy performance benchmarks. |

**Parallelism:** A, B and D can proceed concurrently with the existing C work, provided their declared file scopes remain disjoint. Release preparation and test-runner analysis are also independent. **E should sequence shared-file edits with B and C**—particularly `codex_app_server.py`, `ui.py` and `app.js`. Serialize deployment through F.

Three integration details matter:

- The **scope-overlap fix already exists** in commit `8b5e5d4`, but is unintegrated. Extract that repair carefully: its older recovery changes should not override newer Stop safeguards.
- The **SQLite startup patch already exists in the working tree**. Preserve and evaluate it rather than rewriting it or accidentally including unrelated changes.
- The **mobile HTML implementation is now active**. Its status changed during the audit; it is no longer merely a proposal.

There are also separate decisions and cleanup:

- **Lead succession/inherited supervision** remains an open design issue in its [existing thread](agentcoord://thread/cb9f95c4-0ead-41e3-8314-d9ec3a3aa5a6). Keep it adjacent to lifecycle work, without making a broad redesign a prerequisite for targeted fixes.
- **Live backend replacement during continuous work remains explicitly paused.** Ordinary safe-idle handover already works.
- **Stale queued message #14130 needs cleanup**, but withdrawal functionality exists through closure-message suppression.
- **Wakes after the OKC stand-down came from scheduler nudges and subsequent messages.** That is a workflow problem; I found no proof that durable Stop was bypassed.

I retained, but did **not** promote to confirmed defects: scoped waiting-state friction, opaque diagnostics after tool rejection, unexplained original Antigravity interruptions, undated bookkeeping errors, and previously unreproduced button failures.

I excluded already-resolved incidents—including the Claude false disconnect, ordinary send/open latency, gray Send, several navigation/mobile issues, and runtime-routing fixes—as well as external provider capacity/quota failures. No single agent broke. Several rules that each look reasonable alone worked against each other, and the backend's update rule made your rollout request impossible without stopping the agents. Ranked by how much damage each did:

**1. Agents were told not to use Git, while about 12 of them edited one shared copy of the repo.**
- The beads startup text said "no git operations", which contradicted CLAUDE.md's "commit your changes". The orchestrator followed beads: at 15:26 it listed "resolve the no-Git restriction" as a release step, and at 16:48 it told the UI agent "No … Git operations."
- At 13:15 an install test copied half-finished code from that shared copy into the live plugin caches. After that, nobody trusted the shared copy either.
- That left no commits and no trusted working copy. The only way to pin "the version that was approved" was to copy the files and record their hashes. That's where the patch folders, the 19 GB, the drift from main, and "rebuilding everything from scratch" came from. The Mobile HTML agent re-applied six patches onto a copy of build 20 because no commit existed to build from.
- The beads instruction was removed at 17:02 (commit e7c5c20). The shared-copy problem is still there.

**2. The backend can only update when the whole app is idle.**
- The handover check refuses while any agent anywhere has a running turn or a pending permission prompt.
- With a fleet running all day, that never happens. The backend has been the same one since 02:23, and five newer ones have been staged since. Another one appeared while I was writing this, and the runtime still reports `admitted operations, active turns`.
- AGENTS.md also says not to stop agents to force the update. So agents kept replying "staged, waiting for a safe idle point" instead of telling you plainly: this can't happen unless you stop work.

**3. The interface updates immediately, but the backend doesn't.**
- When a build is installed, the new web pages go live right away while the old backend keeps running. Build 21 added a new file, `permission-menu.js`, which the old backend refuses to serve, so the app crashed.
- The reviewer tested against a test server, not against the old backend.

**4. The skills push agents to reuse long-lived agents and to review everything independently.**
- The orchestrate skill says to reuse agents that already have context, keep a long-lived owner for release and UI work, and reuse a dedicated release agent.
- So the orchestrator turned yesterday's "Updating without interrupting agents" discussion into the release owner. The mobile HTML bug thread became the UI integrator and installer, and the responsiveness agent kept getting new work at 388M tokens.
- The skill also pairs every implementer with an independent reviewer, so each change went author → reviewer → orchestrator → release owner → validator.
- The result was 845 messages between agents since 11:40, 196 of which woke an agent up. Most weren't needed: only 179 asked for a reply, and 288 were purely informational.
- The orchestrator handled 172 incoming messages in one conversation, and its writing visibly degraded by the afternoon.

**5. Two coordinators, and nobody owned "ship everything that's done."**
- The dispatcher sent your UI requests to individual agents. The orchestrator ran a reliability-only campaign and froze a reliability-only release.
- Build 19 left out all the UI work, and nobody flagged it until you noticed at 16:45. Build 21 was the scramble to fix that.

**6. Checks meant for a public release were applied to a local install.**
- After your 15:30 "stop and ship," every delay was a test problem, not a product bug:
  - a permissions problem in a frozen copy of the tests;
  - a timing race in a test fixture;
  - a 90-second native UI test timeout.
- Each one triggered another full test run and another independent re-check, with a round of messages each time.

**7. Your own instruction made items 4 and 6 worse.** At 13:03 you asked them to "make sure we independently review and validate them." The agents read that in the strictest possible way and never asked how much checking a local install actually needed.

The "context collapse" you saw is real, but it's a symptom. Each agent was mostly following its rules; the rules conflicted, and the runtime couldn't do what you asked.

**Smallest changes that would have prevented most of today:**
1. Give each agent its own Git worktree and branch, and build only from a named commit. That removes the snapshot folders, the drift and the rebuilds.
2. Make the backend handover drain instead of waiting for global idle: new turns start on the new backend while old ones finish. Until then, have agents say plainly that rolling out means stopping work.
3. Don't let the new interface go live until its backend is live, or have the old backend serve files from the new bundle.
4. Change the orchestrate and dispatch skills: use fresh agents for new roles, make messages not ask for a reply by default, and have one owner for "what ships."

No single agent broke. Several rules that each look reasonable alone worked against each other, and the backend's update rule made your rollout request impossible without stopping the agents. Ranked by how much damage each did:

**1. Agents were told not to use Git, while about 12 of them edited one shared copy of the repo.**
- The beads startup text said "no git operations", which contradicted CLAUDE.md's "commit your changes". The orchestrator followed beads: at 15:26 it listed "resolve the no-Git restriction" as a release step, and at 16:48 it told the UI agent "No … Git operations."
- At 13:15 an install test copied half-finished code from that shared copy into the live plugin caches. After that, nobody trusted the shared copy either.
- That left no commits and no trusted working copy. The only way to pin "the version that was approved" was to copy the files and record their hashes. That's where the patch folders, the 19 GB, the drift from main, and "rebuilding everything from scratch" came from. The Mobile HTML agent re-applied six patches onto a copy of build 20 because no commit existed to build from.
- The beads instruction was removed at 17:02 (commit e7c5c20). The shared-copy problem is still there.

**2. The backend can only update when the whole app is idle.**
- The handover check refuses while any agent anywhere has a running turn or a pending permission prompt.
- With a fleet running all day, that never happens. The backend has been the same one since 02:23, and five newer ones have been staged since. Another one appeared while I was writing this, and the runtime still reports `admitted operations, active turns`.
- AGENTS.md also says not to stop agents to force the update. So agents kept replying "staged, waiting for a safe idle point" instead of telling you plainly: this can't happen unless you stop work.

**3. The interface updates immediately, but the backend doesn't.**
- When a build is installed, the new web pages go live right away while the old backend keeps running. Build 21 added a new file, `permission-menu.js`, which the old backend refuses to serve, so the app crashed.
- The reviewer tested against a test server, not against the old backend.

**4. The skills push agents to reuse long-lived agents and to review everything independently.**
- The orchestrate skill says to reuse agents that already have context, keep a long-lived owner for release and UI work, and reuse a dedicated release agent.
- So the orchestrator turned yesterday's "Updating without interrupting agents" discussion into the release owner. The mobile HTML bug thread became the UI integrator and installer, and the responsiveness agent kept getting new work at 388M tokens.
- The skill also pairs every implementer with an independent reviewer, so each change went author → reviewer → orchestrator → release owner → validator.
- The result was 845 messages between agents since 11:40, 196 of which woke an agent up. Most weren't needed: only 179 asked for a reply, and 288 were purely informational.
- The orchestrator handled 172 incoming messages in one conversation, and its writing visibly degraded by the afternoon.

**5. Two coordinators, and nobody owned "ship everything that's done."**
- The dispatcher sent your UI requests to individual agents. The orchestrator ran a reliability-only campaign and froze a reliability-only release.
- Build 19 left out all the UI work, and nobody flagged it until you noticed at 16:45. Build 21 was the scramble to fix that.

**6. Checks meant for a public release were applied to a local install.**
- After your 15:30 "stop and ship," every delay was a test problem, not a product bug:
  - a permissions problem in a frozen copy of the tests;
  - a timing race in a test fixture;
  - a 90-second native UI test timeout.
- Each one triggered another full test run and another independent re-check, with a round of messages each time.

**7. Your own instruction made items 4 and 6 worse.** At 13:03 you asked them to "make sure we independently review and validate them." The agents read that in the strictest possible way and never asked how much checking a local install actually needed.

The "context collapse" you saw is real, but it's a symptom. Each agent was mostly following its rules; the rules conflicted, and the runtime couldn't do what you asked.

**Smallest changes that would have prevented most of today:**
1. Give each agent its own Git worktree and branch, and build only from a named commit. That removes the snapshot folders, the drift and the rebuilds.
2. Make the backend handover drain instead of waiting for global idle: new turns start on the new backend while old ones finish. Until then, have agents say plainly that rolling out means stopping work.
3. Don't let the new interface go live until its backend is live, or have the old backend serve files from the new bundle.
4. Change the orchestrate and dispatch skills: use fresh agents for new roles, make messages not ask for a reply by default, and have one owner for "what ships."

evidence.text:
**The robust fix is to make the runtime own writes, make reads genuinely read-only, and isolate each conversation’s persistence dependencies.** I’d keep SQLite: WAL supports concurrent readers, but permits only one writer at a time. The application should explicitly manage that serialization. [SQLite documentation](https://sqlite.org/wal.html#concurrency)

There are five connected changes:

1. **Give the runtime sole responsibility for database mutations and migrations.**  
   CLI commands, hooks, and monitors should send mutations to the existing runtime through authenticated local requests. Currently, they use the runtime’s *code* but still write from separate processes. Run versioned migrations once during startup or upgrade; ordinary commands should only check compatibility. Preserve the existing ownership lock when starting a runtime.

2. **Enforce read-only query paths.**  
   Thread lists, history, metadata, and close-status queries should use database connections that reject writes. Move initialization, reconciliation, and implicit updates out of those paths. Opening a conversation should display its saved/current snapshot without waiting for provider startup or database maintenance.

3. **Move persistence off shared locks and provider event processing.**  
   Capture a conversation’s state under a short lock, then serialize and save it outside that lock. A dedicated writer should use short transactions, bounded queues, and fair scheduling. Repeated history snapshots can be combined into the latest version; lifecycle events and user commands must retain their required ordering.

4. **Replace the global “flush everything” gate with per-conversation ordering.**  
   Sending in conversation A should wait only for A’s necessary prior state. Use sequence numbers and turn identities so an old completion cannot overwrite a newer turn. Persist command acceptance before acknowledging it, retain request IDs for duplicate detection, and reconcile uncertain provider submissions after crashes rather than blindly resending them.

5. **Give observers an efficient data interface.**  
   The attention monitor should fetch metadata in batches and consume activity incrementally using a cursor. Cache unchanged metadata and bound concurrency. That reduces load, while the backend changes ensure a busy observer cannot monopolize the application.

I’d deliver the read-path and shared-lock fixes first, then complete write ownership and conversation-scoped persistence. Increasing timeouts would leave the underlying dependencies intact.

**The acceptance tests matter as much as the implementation:**

- Hold a database write transaction open: existing conversation reads must remain responsive.
- Stall persistence for A: B must still open, and B’s actions must not depend on A’s queue draining.
- Run the observed monitor workload alongside streaming agents and multiple windows.
- Kill/restart during acceptance and persistence: retain acknowledged work and prevent duplicate submission.
- Meet the existing latency budgets under that load, while recording transaction duration, queue age, lock waits, and request latency.

This is the proposed repair design; implementation and deployment are still outstanding.

excerpt_windows.text:
outs live: installing a new build (local rebuild or Sparkle update) must put new runtime code into service within 60 seconds regardless of agent activity, without stopping, restarting, or interrupting any agent. Today a backend change waits until every agent is idle at the same moment; with agents running continuously that never happens, so shipping a fix means stopping everything. I develop Ribbon Field with Ribbon Field agents running all day, and customers running long pipelines face the same choice on every update. I want the robust long-term design, not the smallest patch.

Context
- Contract and current design: docs/runtime-updates.md. Single-owner, idle-boundary handover was a first-release scope; you may revise it, but keep its safety invariants and update the document to match what you ship.
- Why rollouts block: in plugins/agent-coord/scripts/agent_coord/desktop_runtime.py, `schema_fingerprint()` hashes every module, so any .py change requires the idle boundary. `busy_reasons()` counts active turns, pending approvals, admitted operations, and in-flight review/dispatch/queue/app-control rows across all agents. `Runtime.serve()` performs the handover and already passes the owner lock fd to the candidate via `pass_fds`.
- Why "swap now" currently means "kill": codex_app_server.py, claude_code.py, and acp.py launch providers as runtime children speaking JSON-RPC/stream-json over stdio pipes, with pending request futures and reader threads in memory. Those pipes die with the runtime. Native resume (`thread/resume`, `claude --resume`) starts a new turn; that is recovery, not an uninterrupted turn.
- Already rejected: a bounded drain (hold new work, wait for idle, abandon after a deadline) still waits on agents. The existing `pause` also blocks approval answers and disables the watchdog.
- Build, install, and rollout rules: CLAUDE.md, desktop/macos/README.md ("Build and install locally"), docs/reference.md (plugin refresh). Prior signed-replacement harness and findings: build/macos/update-validation-recovery/.
- You are probably running inside the runtime you will replace. Plan for that.

Bar
- With at least three agents mid-turn across Codex and Claude (one streaming, one inside a long tool call, one waiting on an approval, ideally one waiting on a child agent), installing a build with different backend code puts it in service within 60 s, shown by the active payload digest in runtime status.
- No provider process is killed, signaled, or restarted by a rollout. Every running turn completes as the same turn; streamed output has no gaps or duplicates; any UI-visible stall stays under 5 s. An approval answered after the swap reaches its original request. Queued, scheduled, and inbox work dispatches exactly once. CLI, hooks, and MCP route to the new payload afterward.
- Repeatable: 50 consecutive swaps under continuous fake-provider load with zero interruptions or invariant violations.
- Failure never escalates: a candidate that fails to start, crashes at any handover step, or is incompatible leaves the current runtime and every agent running, and the failure is reported. Never two owners of the queue, scheduler, or inbox; never a fallback to killing work.
- Replace the hash-everything rule with an explicit compatibility contract. Keep whatever owns the provider pipes minimal and rarely changed; define and test what happens when it does change, and state plainly any change class that still needs a boundary. Database changes follow expand/contract so routine migrations never force idle.

Approach
This problem has established solutions. Before committing, evaluate at least two architectures against the bar with a measured spike, for example: (a) in-place handover, where the old runtime passes provider pipe fds (SCM_RIGHTS/`pass_fds`) and serialized session state to the new one (nginx/HAProxy binary upgrade, Envoy hot restart, systemd fd store); (b) a minimal, stable host per provider process that owns its pipes and exposes a reconnectable, sequence-numbered, acknowledged event stream (tmux/dtach/abduco), letting the coordinator restart at any time. Erlang/OTP `code_change` state transfer and Temporal worker versioning are also worth reading. Record the decision, the measurements behind it, and the rejected alternative in docs/runtime-updates.md, then proceed; the design does not need my approval.

Verification
- Deterministic tests on isolated databases, runtime directories, and fake providers for each mid-turn state above, with fault injection at every handover step (candidate crash, SIGKILL of either side mid-transfer, stale discovery, incompatible protocol). Fake providers record every tool invocation and output sequence number so duplicates and gaps are detectable.
- The 50-swap soak with its invariant report.
- `python3 -W error::ResourceWarning -m unittest discover -s tests -v`, the JavaScript tests, and plugin packaging validation.
- Extend the signed-replacement harness: a v1-to-v2 Sparkle update with active turns now swaps the backend live instead of waiting for idle.
- A separate agent reviews the diff and runs its own checks.
- Live proof on my laptop, after I approve it: drive the first live swap from a process that does not depend on the runtime (detached controller or terminal session). Then roll out a trivial backend change from inside a Ribbon Field conversation while other agents are mid-turn, and show that all of them, including that conversation, continue.
- Do not modify tests, harnesses, or fake providers to make checks pass. If something misses the bar or cannot be verified, say so plainly with the measurements you did get.

Constraints and autonomy
- Never stop, kill, or restart my running agents, including during testing. Ever

An approval answered after the swap reaches its original request. Queued, scheduled, and inbox work dispatches exactly once. CLI, hooks, and MCP route to the new payload afterward.
- Repeatable: 50 consecutive swaps under continuous fake-provider load with zero interruptions or invariant violations.
- Failure never escalates: a candidate that fails to start, crashes at any handover step, or is incompatible leaves the current runtime and every agent running, and the failure is reported. Never two owners of the queue, scheduler, or inbox; never a fallback to killing work.
- Replace the hash-everything rule with an explicit compatibility contract. Keep whatever owns the provider pipes minimal and rarely changed; define and test what happens when it does change, and state plainly any change class that still needs a boundary. Database changes follow expand/contract so routine migrations never force idle.

Approach
This problem has established solutions. Before committing, evaluate at least two architectures against the bar with a measured spike, for example: (a) in-place handover, where the old runtime passes provider pipe fds (SCM_RIGHTS/`pass_fds`) and serialized session state to the new one (nginx/HAProxy binary upgrade, Envoy hot restart, systemd fd store); (b) a minimal, stable host per provider process that owns its pipes and exposes a reconnectable, sequence-numbered, acknowledged event stream (tmux/dtach/abduco), letting the coordinator restart at any time. Erlang/OTP `code_change` state transfer and Temporal worker versioning are also worth reading. Record the decision, the measurements behind it, and the rejected alternative in docs/runtime-updates.md, then proceed; the design does not need my approval.

Verification
- Deterministic tests on isolated databases, runtime directories, and fake providers for each mid-turn state above, with fault injection at every handover step (candidate crash, SIGKILL of either side mid-transfer, stale discovery, incompatible protocol). Fake providers record every tool invocation and output sequence number so duplicates and gaps are detectable.
- The 50-swap soak with its invariant report.
- `python3 -W error::ResourceWarning -m unittest discover -s tests -v`, the JavaScript tests, and plugin packaging validation.
- Extend the signed-replacement harness: a v1-to-v2 Sparkle update with active turns now swaps the backend live instead of waiting for idle.
- A separate agent reviews the diff and runs its own checks.
- Live proof on my laptop, after I approve it: drive the first live swap from a process that does not depend on the runtime (detached controller or terminal session). Then roll out a trivial backend change from inside a Ribbon Field conversation while other agents are mid-turn, and show that all of them, including that conversation, continue.
- Do not modify tests, harnesses, or fake providers to make checks pass. If something misses the bar or cannot be verified, say so plainly with the measurements you did get.

Constraints and autonomy
- Never stop, kill, or restart my running agents, including during testing. Everything before the live proof uses isolated state.
- Ask me once, immediately before the first live swap with real agents, and before any public release or feed publication. Local installs and commits are fine; choose a version/build newer than the installed one.
- Keep the contract's invariants: authenticated local-user-only control, no root daemon or login item, macOS 12, both architectures. Preserve CLI/plugin/skill identifiers, bundle ID, and saved-data paths.
- Follow CLAUDE.md: begin-work scope when other sessions are active, plugin refresh after plugin changes, commit when done.

Deliverable
Commits on main, the updated docs/runtime-updates.md, and the acceptance harness. A short report: what an agent experiences during a swap (measured stall p50/p95/max), what still needs a boundary and why, soak and fault-injection results, live-proof evidence (payload digests before and after, agent transcripts), and open limitations.

The author's own tests pass on it (230 Python, 45 JavaScript); I tested against fake providers only.

**F1 (blocking): a retry can send the user's prompt twice.**
- Before retrying, the code removes the rejected turn from Codex's history. It then confirms the removal by checking the turn is absent from the list of turns in Codex's reply.
- Codex's protocol definition says that list is always empty in this reply, so the confirmation always passes.
- The author's fake provider returns the full list, which real Codex doesn't, so no test catches it.
- I reproduced it: a fake that answers the way real Codex does, without actually removing anything, leaves two copies of the prompt in the provider's history.
- Fix: after removing the turn, re-read the history from Codex and confirm the rejected turn is gone. If that read fails or doesn't match, treat it as uncertain and don't resend. The fake should also answer the way real Codex does.

**F2 (should fix): a rejected message cancels the pending retry.** If the user sends a message while a retry is waiting and that message is refused ("Your draft was not sent"), the retry is cancelled anyway. The original request silently dies. Cancellation should only happen once the new message is accepted.

evidence.text:
I approved the combined UI delivery (message 16236) with no blocking findings. It bundles six feature patches on top of the installed 0.1.4 build 20, and the exact version I approved is `5c45d51d…`.

**How it was put together:**
- I rebuilt it myself from the original files plus the six patches. The result matches the candidate byte for byte, so nothing was overwritten with stale files.
- Its starting point is exactly the installed build 20.
- None of the patches touch the reliability-critical code, and the earlier fixes (I09, I10, I23 and my two chat fixes) are all present.

**Permission modes:** this is the one patch with real backend weight, since it changes how much each AI provider may do without asking.
- Old conversations get the same permissions as before.
- An explicitly chosen mode isn't reset by unrelated settings changes.
- Kimi and Antigravity refuse to start a turn if the provider didn't actually apply the chosen mode.
- The focused permission and provider tests pass, along with 252 tests for the changed UI areas.

**The actual UI:** I tested it in a desktop browser (Chromium) and a phone browser (WebKit) using the author's test setup with simulated AI providers. There were no page errors.
- Copying a code block works.
- A text selection survives incoming streamed text.
- "Discuss" adds a quote to your draft without sending it.
- Title autosave works when you click away.
- The context sidebar hides its tabs when there's no agent family.
- The thread menu works on desktop and through the "⋯" sheet on phones.
- The permission menu works on both, with blocked modes greyed out and locked while a turn runs.
- The new List overview renders correctly.

Screenshots and results are in `build/ui-delivery-review-ad9c/qa/`.

**Notes, none blocking:**
- **Rollback risk:** older backends only understand "YOLO on/off". If the app ever falls back to one, a conversation set to a stricter mode would run with the older default, which allows edits and asks first, so it would have more access than chosen. That belongs in the rollout notes.
- **Unverified mode change:** Antigravity treats a mode change as applied even when it can't confirm it.
- **Stray cache files:** the author's own test run left about 137 Python cache files in the candidate folder; the build should leave them out.
- **Backend not yet switched:** the running backend is still on an older version with a newer one pending, so installing the app alone won't activate these backend changes.

**Not tested:** real provider menus (the test used simulated providers), long-press on a physical iPhone, and reading the phone browser's clipboard back. I didn't run the full test suites, since the author runs those.

Next I'll verify the build, the installed version and the active backend when the rollout is delivered.

contradictions_and_distinctions.claim: SSE stream duration caused Networking memory growth
contradictions_and_distinctions.evidence: Oct28 user window reload left memory unchanged; isolated WebKit lab found approximately5.5KB retention per fetch regardless of stream/connection/storage. Request count reduction4b43720 replaced stream recycling.

contradictions_and_distinctions.claim: Fast isolated detail GETs prove the recurring timeout is absent
contradictions_and_distinctions.evidence: Oct31 stall diagnosis measured16–198ms direct GETs and a24-request burst without reproducing, then captured142percentCPU during a renewed UI stall. Current33second tail readings require contextual attribution.

contradictions_and_distinctions.claim: All prior fixes failed or were never active
contradictions_and_distinctions.evidence: Oct29 owner explicitly verified build17 backend activation07:24UTC and live improvement. Later failures do not erase that measurement.

contradictions_and_distinctions.claim: Installed app version equals active backend
contradictions_and_distinctions.evidence: Build19 installed while17 active; build34 installed while30 active; build42 installed while41 active. Conversation records distinguish these states.

contradictions_and_distinctions.claim: All stalls are one identical software defect
contradictions_and_distinctions.evidence: History/shared-runtime/database/polling defects overlap, but Oct31 low-battery throttling and WebKit request retention are distinct mechanisms; collateral runtime-control failures require independent causal linking.
